# Local adaptive toolbar extensions

Source: adaptive_platform_ui 1.0.2, https://pub.dev/packages/adaptive_platform_ui. License retained. UPSTREAM_SHA256.json records original upstream inputs.

Opt-in API: AdaptiveApp.androidToolbarBackend (also router constructor) supplies AndroidToolbarBackend(builder, height, supports). AdaptiveToolbarHost installs this backend alongside the existing registry. The framework has no dependency on Deadliner, Compose or the app MethodChannel protocol.

AdaptiveScaffold publishes androidNativeToolbar and the actual per-page scrollOffset in ToolbarEntry, suppresses a supported Material AppBar, and provides measured status/content insets through AndroidToolbarBodyScope. Default bodies are padded safely; extendBodyBehindAppBar clients put the supplied inset inside scroll content. Native pages publish transparent system bars and theme-aware icon brightness when there is no Flutter AppBar.

No backend, unsupported app bars, drawers, non-page scaffolds or useNativeToolbar=false retain the Material path. The app defines support policy and owns the native bridge. iOS uses the original HostedTopToolbar → IOS26NativeToolbar → UINavigationBar path with useNativeToolbar=true, with structured native content support described below. Existing hosted iOS toolbar and registry tests pass with the optional extension absent. debugAndroidToolbar is a test-only host switch because PlatformInfo uses dart:io rather than Flutter platform overrides.

AdaptiveScaffold.fallbackBuilder keeps custom/original Material page rendering in the same toolbar registry. Body wrappers remain stable across backend changes so form and scroll state survive the preference toggle. The application-facing AdaptiveUI facade owns all backend selection and exposes AdaptiveTopAppBar to pages. Upstream tests, screenshots and exploration documentation are omitted from this vendored runtime package.

AdaptiveScaffold.fallbackUsesNativeToolbar lets an application-provided Scaffold retain a Flutter footer while the registered backend owns the complete toolbar. The custom scaffold must omit its AppBar in this mode.

The iOS toolbar factory has an opt-in nativeTitleLayout/updateConfiguration contract: UINavigationBar owns all chrome, UILabel/UIControl own plain or double-line tappable titles, and UIBarButtonItem/UIActivityIndicatorView own actions and pending states. The timetable title hides iOS 26 shared button chrome and supplies its full intrinsic width. The existing hosted-toolbar behavior is unchanged when this contract is absent. Scroll-only updates adjust a shared native UIVisualEffectView without recreating titles and actions. HostedTopToolbar forwards this structured configuration through IOS26NativeToolbar on all supported iOS versions. It omits Flutter title/back-button/backdrop overlays for this mode; the original host continues to own route blending and toolbar registration. There is no separate app-owned UIKit toolbar host; iOS top bars remain UIKit when the original-component preference is enabled. SF Symbols and title/action callbacks are mapped inside AdaptiveUI, never in page platform branches.

Ordinary component integration is owned by lib/AdaptiveUI. Android uses flutter_miuix 1.3.0, iOS continues to use this package, and the original-component preference keeps platform defaults available. The SDK floor is Dart 3.12.2 as required by flutter_miuix. Top bars retain the native Compose/UIKit paths. Text input forwards editing-complete, suggestion, autofill and outside-tap contracts; AdaptiveUI keeps FormField state and controllers outside the selected editor. Unsupported MIUIX editing hooks retain the default editor. Android dialogs use MiuixOverlayDialog inside their existing Flutter DialogRoute, with one barrier and preserved results. A modal retains its renderer until dismissal so arbitrary form state survives preference changes; the next opening uses the new preference.

Color ownership remains in AdaptiveUI. Hosted iOS toolbars resolve explicit light/dark mode through CupertinoTheme (rather than the device brightness), and structured native titles receive the shared foreground color. Cards receive the application surfaceContainer token. Native platform styling and existing component contracts are preserved.

Shared page design is defined by AdaptivePageList/AdaptivePageScroll/AdaptivePageFrame and AdaptiveSection in the application facade: 16dp gutters and section gaps, a 760dp content column, flat semantic cards with HyperOS neutral colors, Android 20dp and iOS 16dp corners. iOS grouped rows retain inset dividers. Renderer choice remains inside AdaptiveUI. AdaptiveDropdown bounds its trailing value, wraps complete menu labels, and keeps MIUIX menus in the Flutter Navigator overlay with viewport/keyboard-aware placement. The Material fallback follows the same width policy. An open MIUIX menu registers a PopScope on its owning route, so system and native-toolbar back close the menu before navigating away. AdaptiveDropdownFormField preserves FormField validation and controller ownership.

Home navigation is composed by the application AdaptiveNavigationShell. iOS 26 uses this package's existing IOS26NativeTabBar/UITabBar, older iOS uses CupertinoTabBar, and Android backend selection remains in AdaptiveUI. Native tab brightness follows the app's explicit CupertinoTheme rather than device mode. UITabBar exposes bounded diagnostics and item activation for integration verification; activation calls the real native selection delegate. Retained offstage tabs relinquish toolbar ownership, route/keyboard visibility hides the bottom chrome, and shared content wrappers reserve its scroll clearance once.

The home host reserves UITabBar's measured intrinsic height through onHeightChanged instead of forcing a 64pt frame. Native width changes request a new fit, preserving UIKit's icon/label layout after initial mounting or rotation; the application updates content clearance from the same measurement.

Android bottom navigation is now an Activity-owned Compose sibling of Flutter, selected inside AdaptiveUI. A geometry/selection channel replaces the bottom PlatformView and its hybrid-composition gesture path; native pointer routing targets only the actual chrome bounds. Semantics actions remain in Flutter. iOS continues to use the unchanged UIKit tab renderer. The shared wrappers consume bottom clearance in scroll padding, while the timetable viewport extends behind the floating chrome. Timetable/week-page futures and profile metadata are retained across unrelated rebuilds and invalidated by their actual model/viewport inputs.

Material bottom navigation is mounted outside Scaffold.bottomNavigationBar, so AdaptiveUI removes only its inherited top padding before building NavigationBar. NavigationBar itself consumes the navigation inset once; there is no outer bottom SafeArea or extra vertical margin. Its content height and the shared clearance are both 64dp. This prevents the status-bar inset appearing as a blank band above destinations, including on devices with tall status areas or three-button navigation.

The home tab bar leaves unselected tint unset so UIKit chooses its dynamic foreground. IOS26NativeTabBar forwards a non-null-to-null tint update to setStyle; the native view clears unselectedItemTintColor and rebuilds template symbols to remove previously baked-in colors. Selected tint still follows the app accent.

AdaptiveTypography defines shared content sizes (16 item, 14 body, 13 caption, 15 action) for Material, Flutter MIUIX and iOS content while preserving platform fonts, accessibility scaling and UIKit chrome metrics. AdaptiveListTile retains styled/rich title and subtitle widgets in MIUIX, and Material owns its vertical spacing without duplicate outer padding.

Course summary cards use AdaptivePressable in the application facade. Their arbitrary multiline contents and press feedback stay in Flutter compositing so UIKit platform views cannot punch through a later popup route. Ordinary UIKit buttons and native toolbar contracts remain intact.

AdaptiveTabRow uses the original iOS 26 AdaptiveSegmentedControl → UISegmentedControl path. The state exposes bounded diagnostics and activateNativeSegment for integration tests; activation selects the real native segment and sends valueChanged. The application facade removes the platform view while a popup route or keyboard covers the page, preserving category selection outside it.
